title_en.text: Museo nina Marcela Mariño at Felipe Agoncillo

tagline.text: The old home of the flag-sewing Marcela, a free museum in Taal

children.text: This is the old home of Marcela Mariño and her husband Felipe Agoncillo in Taal Heritage Town. A free national museum run by the NHCP, it tells how the first Philippine flag was sewn in Hong Kong during the Revolution and recounts the life of the country's first diplomat, with a guide.

Walking through Taal Heritage Town, you will find a house on the street that runs south from the Basilica and carries its name. It is the home where Marcela Mariño de Agoncillo and her husband Felipe Agoncillo lived, and it is now a museum run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP),
Museo nina Marcela Mariño at Felipe Agoncillo
. The street is also named after Marcela, and map apps sometimes list the place as "Marcela Agoncillo Historical Landmark."

Marcela is known as the woman who, during the Philippine Revolution in Hong Kong, sewed the first national flag to General Aguinaldo's design together with her daughter Lorenza and Delfina Herbosa de Natividad. Her husband Felipe was born in Taal in 1859, became a lawyer, and is called the "first Filipino diplomat" for his diplomatic work on behalf of the revolutionary government around the 1898 Treaty of Paris negotiations between the United States and Spain. Following their story gives you a close look at the history of independence behind a single flag.

The house is a Spanish colonial-era bahay na bato built of adobe walls and timber. Many accounts say Marcela's grandfather, Don Andrés Mariño, built it in the late 18th century (around the 1770s–1780s), while some older sources give the late 17th century, so the exact year varies by source. Either way, it is counted among the oldest buildings in Taal. On July 6, 1980, Marcela's daughters donated the house, its furniture, and family memorabilia to the government, which led to the public museum.

Admission is free and donations are accepted. A visit takes about an hour, so it fits well as a middle stop on a walking route that links the Basilica, the Caysasay shrine, and other ancestral-house museums in Taal. For Korean travelers, it can be described as the Philippines' own "taegeukgi story." Opening hours and procedures differ from source to source, so please check the latest announcement before you go.
On entering, you first watch a roughly
12-minute

video on the ground floor. It covers Felipe Agoncillo's diplomatic work and the family's exile in Hong Kong. Following staff directions, you wait on a bench and then go in together, so think of it as moving with a group rather than entering individually.

blocks.title: Diorama of the first flag being sewn

children.text: Near the staircase stands a nearly life-size model. It recreates the scene of Marcela, her daughter Lorenza, and Delfina Herbosa stitching the flag. The flag is said to have been finished in about five days. It is the museum's centerpiece.

Flags of the Katipunan and various other flags from the Revolution are on permanent display. You can compare how the flag's design changed over time, so it feels a bit like a flag museum. The museum is described as having seven galleries in all.

The living quarters are on the second floor, where the original narra floorboards remain. You will see capiz-shell windows, a glass chandelier, an antique sewing machine, a long banquet table, and china cabinets. Furniture such as Louis XVI-style pieces and Viennese bentwood chairs are mixed together, showing the tastes of an upper-class household of the time.

A genealogy chart and old books in Tagalog, English, and French are on display. Marcela and Felipe married in 1889 and had six daughters; one died at age three, and the remaining daughters are said not to have married. That is why the house could pass intact, under the family's name, into a museum.

blocks.title: Bronze statue of Marcela in the garden

children.text: In the side garden stands a bronze statue of Marcela raising the flag, unveiled in 1985. Flagpoles with the Katipunan flag and revolutionary flags also stand there. Visitors report that the rear garden has a view toward the Pansipit River.

Visitors report that one more short video plays near the exit. At the end there is a small souvenir corner selling local products such as balisong (a folding knife from nearby towns) keychains. There is no fixed price list, so check prices on the spot.

In front of the house is a marker installed on November 27, 1955, by the National Historical Institute (the predecessor of the NHCP), according to records. This means the place was recognized as a heritage site even before it became a museum. Comparing it with other ancestral houses in Taal helps explain why this house is treated with such importance.

items.title: Taal half-day route
items.subtitle: On foot from the Basilica to the Agoncillo museum

children.text: Taking an early bus from Manila, plan to reach Lemery around
. Opening hours differ by source, so it is best not to arrive late. From Lemery, take a jeepney or tricycle into Taal town.
Start with Taal Plaza and the Basilica of St. Martin of Tours. It is large, so it takes about 30 minutes.
It is about
10 minutes
on foot from the Basilica to the museum. Walk along Calle Marcela Mariño Agoncillo and enjoy the old houses.
Enter the museum, watch the 12-minute video, and tour following the staff's guidance. It usually takes
45 minutes–1 hour
Have lunch at a nearby restaurant. Places such as Don Juan Boodle House and Cuchara y Tenedor are often recommended.
Look around other ancestral houses on the same street, such as Galleria Taal and the Leon Apacible museum.
Go down the San Lorenzo Ruiz Steps (about 125 granite steps) to the Caysasay shrine, then climb back up the steps or take a tricycle.
The museum may close between 4 and 5 p.m., so we recommend visiting it first in the morning.
Leave Manila in the morning, arrive around lunchtime, and see the museum and Galleria Taal.
Stay at a heritage-house lodging and take an evening stroll along the quiet old streets.
Browse the market and check the Basilica's morning Mass times. The Basilica opens early in the morning.
See the Caysasay shrine and steps and the Agoncillo mansion (the White House), then head back.
Take a DLTB bus from Manila (Cubao, Buendia, and elsewhere) to Lemery. Depending on traffic, it takes about
2–3.5 hours
Bus fares vary by source at about ₱220~310, so check on the spot.
From Lemery to Taal town, take a jeepney (about ₱14~16) or a tricycle (about ₱60 one way as listed).
Schedules and fares change often. Check the latest timetable before boarding.

items.title: By private car or rental car from Manila

children.text: Leave the STAR Tollway at Lipa and follow the road toward Taal. Allow more than 2 hours from Manila.
The Diokno Highway route via Tagaytay is scenic, but some guides warn that it has many sharp curves.
Take a Lipa-bound bus from Taft Avenue, Alabang, or elsewhere (about
1.5–2 hours
), get off at the Tambo exit, and transfer to a jeepney to Taal (about
1 hour
The museum is within walking distance of the Basilica, about
away.
Tricycles in town cost about ₱30~50, and longer rides about ₱100~120. It is hot at midday, so bring water and a hat.
The museum is an indoor visit, so you can go year-round. However, Taal involves a lot of walking outdoors, so the November–May dry season is more comfortable.
Volcanic alert levels around Taal Volcano and the lake can change, so check the latest announcements before your visit. Many sources say the museum is closed on Mondays and holidays.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The best time for sightseeing on foot. Tour groups may increase on long weekends and weekends.
Very hot in the daytime, so we recommend visiting in the morning and resting indoors at midday.
Bring an umbrella, and be careful because steps and paved roads can be slippery. The museum interior is little affected.

A day trip is possible, but the old streets of Taal are especially atmospheric at dusk, so many visitors stay overnight. Heritage houses used as lodging, such as Casa Punzalan (about ₱800~2,500) and Paradores del Castillo (from about ₱2,500), are often mentioned. Prices vary greatly by season and room, so check before booking.

For meals, Cuchara y Tenedor (about ₱500~1,000, listed as closed on Mondays), which serves Spanish and Batangas dishes in a 19th-century warehouse, and Don Juan Boodle House (about ₱1,299~1,799, listed as open daily about
), known for its large platters, come up often. Near the market there are balisong knife shops and local snack stalls. Restaurant hours may change.

Opening hours differ slightly by source. Two 2026 guides and a 2021 article on NHCP museums say Tuesday to Sunday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.; some listings give an 8 a.m. opening or a 5 p.m. closing, so go in the morning and avoid Mondays.
The video and tour run for groups, so greet the staff when you arrive and follow their directions.
Even though admission is free, there is a donation box. It helps to have small bills ready.
Follow the posted notices for photography rules inside. Do not touch the exhibits or sit on the furniture.
Taal is very hot in the daytime. Bring an umbrella or parasol, water, a hat, and comfortable shoes.
Combine the museum on foot with the Basilica, Galleria Taal, and the Leon Apacible museum, and allow extra time if you also want to reach the Caysasay shrine, because of the steps.
A balisong is a knife and cannot go in carry-on baggage. If you are flying home, pack it in checked baggage.
The commentary may be in English or Filipino, so reading up on the flag and the Agoncillo couple's story beforehand makes it easier to follow.
Opening hours and days differ by source (closed Mondays and holidays as listed), so check the latest NHCP announcement before visiting. The times in this guide are not confirmed.
Bus fares and schedules change often. Check at the terminal before boarding.
Volcanic alert levels around Taal can change. Check PHIVOLCS announcements before you leave.
Watch for heatstroke in the daytime and drink water often.
In crowded markets and plazas, carry your belongings in front of you.
It is an old wooden building, so the stairs may be steep and the floor slippery. Take care.
This is the old town center that the museum belongs to. The Basilica, plaza, and old houses follow one after another, about
10 minutes
away on foot.

from the museum along the same street, opens every day from early morning.

blocks.title: Galleria Taal and the Leon Apacible Museum

children.text: These are ancestral-house museums on the same street. The Leon Apacible museum is run by the NHCP, and Galleria Taal is listed at about ₱130.

blocks.title: Caysasay shrine and San Lorenzo Ruiz Steps

children.text: Go down about 125 granite steps to reach the Shrine of Our Lady of Caysasay, which is free to enter.
